"'''Venus'''" is a [[song]] written by Ed Marshall and popularized by [[Frankie Avalon]], whose recording was released in 1959 and spent five weeks at number one on the [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]]. The lyrics detail a man's plea to [[Venus (mythology)|Venus]], the [[Roman mythology|Roman]] goddess of love and beauty, to send him a girl to love and one who will love him as well.

"Venus" is a song written by Ed Marshall and popularized by Frankie Avalon, whose recording was released in 1959 and spent five weeks at number one on the Billboard Hot 100. The lyrics detail a man's plea to Venus, the Roman goddess of love and beauty, to send him a girl to love and one who will love him as well.

sections.heading: 1959 version
sections.wikitext: Songwriter Ed Marshall first offered "Venus" to [[Al Martino]], who liked it but only felt it qualified as an album cut. Marshall then played it on the piano for Frankie Avalon, who recalled, "I listened to it, and the first time it just caught me immediately." He recorded it three days later with producers Peter De Angelis and [[Bob Marcucci]]. In a live telephone interview on ''[[American Bandstand]]'' a couple of days afterward, Avalon told [[Dick Clark]] that it would be a hit. The single was released a week later.<ref>{{Harvnb|Bronson|2003|p=50}}</ref>
sections.text: Songwriter Ed Marshall first offered "Venus" to Al Martino, who liked it but only felt it qualified as an album cut. Marshall then played it on the piano for Frankie Avalon, who recalled, "I listened to it, and the first time it just caught me immediately." He recorded it three days later with producers Peter De Angelis and Bob Marcucci. In a live telephone interview on American Bandstand a couple of days afterward, Avalon told Dick Clark that it would be a hit. The single was released a week later.

sections.heading: Chart performance
sections.wikitext: "Venus" debuted on [[Billboard (magazine)|''Billboard'']] magazine's [[Billboard Hot 100|Hot 100]] chart in the issue dated February 9, 1959, and reached number one in the March 9 issue, four weeks later. It spent a total of 28 weeks on the chart, five of which were in the top spot.<ref name = Hot/> The song also reached number 10 on the magazine's [[Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs|R&B chart]].<ref name = "Avalon">{{cite magazine|url= https://www.billboard.com/artist/frankie-avalon/chart-history/hsi/ |title=Frankie Avalon - Chart History (Hot 100)|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |access-date=April 16, 2026 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20211117214907/https://www.billboard.com/artist/frankie-avalon/chart-history/hsi/ | archive-date=November 17, 2021}} For R&B chart information, select Hot R&B/Hip-Hop Songs from the drop-down list.</ref> The magazine ranked it as the number four song for 1959.<ref name = "Year">{{cite magazine |url=https://worldradiohistory.com/Archive-Billboard/Billboard-Spotlight/Billboard-Spotlight-Record-Programming-1959-12-14.pdf |title=Top Sides of 1959-Hot 100 of the year|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|The Billboard]] |date=December 14, 1959 |page=78}}</ref>
sections.text: "Venus" debuted on Billboard magazine's Hot 100 chart in the issue dated February 9, 1959, and reached number one in the March 9 issue, four weeks later. It spent a total of 28 weeks on the chart, five of which were in the top spot. The song also reached number 10 on the magazine's R&B chart. The magazine ranked it as the number four song for 1959.

sections.heading: 1976 version
sections.wikitext: In 1976, Avalon released a new [[disco]] version of "Venus" that was Avalon's last [[Billboard Hot 100|''Billboard'' Hot 100]] hit, peaking at number 46 there<ref name = "FABH">{{cite magazine | title= Billboard Hot 100 | author=<!--Staff writer(s); no by-line.--> |magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |date=March 6, 1976 |page= 68 |issn= 0006-2510 |url= https://www.worldradiohistory.com/Archive-All-Music/Billboard/70s/1976/Billboard%201976-03-06.pdf |access-date= June 19, 2018}}</ref> and at number one on the magazine's [[Hot Adult Contemporary|Easy Listening]] chart.<ref name = "FAEL">{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2007|p=25}}.</ref> Avalon was quoted as saying of the remake: "It was all right, but I still prefer the original."<ref name="hyatt">{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=8ZxHAAAAMAAJ |title=The Billboard Book of Adult Contemporary Hits |first=Wesley |last=Hyatt |date= 1999|isbn=9780823076932 |publisher=Billboard Books}}</ref>
sections.text: In 1976, Avalon released a new disco version of "Venus" that was Avalon's last Billboard Hot 100 hit, peaking at number 46 there and at number one on the magazine's Easy Listening chart. Avalon was quoted as saying of the remake: "It was all right, but I still prefer the original."

sections.heading: Other charting versions
sections.wikitext:
*[[Dickie Valentine]] enter the [[UK singles chart]] on March 19, 1959, with his recording and got as high as number 20 during his eight weeks there.<ref>{{cite web |title= Dickie Valentine |url= https://www.officialcharts.com/artist/401/dickie-valentine/ |access-date=April 17, 2026 |website=Official Charts |language=en}}</ref>
*[[Johnny Mathis]] reached number 23 on ''Billboard''{{'}}s [[Adult Contemporary (chart)|Easy Listening]] chart<ref name = "adult">{{cite magazine|url=https://www.billboard.com/artist/johnny-mathis/chart-history/asi/|title=Johnny Mathis - Chart History (Adult Contemporary)|magazine=[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]] |access-date=November 18, 2025 | archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20251118155530/https://www.billboard.com/artist/johnny-mathis/chart-history/asi/ | archive-date=November 18, 2025}}</ref> and "[[Bubbling Under Hot 100 Singles|bubbled under]]" the ''Billboard'' Hot 100 chart to number 111 in 1968.<ref>{{Harvnb|Whitburn|2009|p=628}}</ref>
*[[Jamie Redfern]] peaked at number 9 on the [[Go-Set]] Australian charts in 1973.<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.poparchives.com.au/gosetcharts/1973/19730714.html#albums |title=Go-Set Australian Charts – July 14, 1973 |publisher=poparchives.com.au |access-date=April 17, 2026 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130513135106/http://www.poparchives.com.au/gosetcharts/1973/19730714.html#albums |archive-date=May 13, 2013}}</ref>
sections.text:
*Dickie Valentine enter the UK singles chart on March 19, 1959, with his recording and got as high as number 20 during his eight weeks there.
*Johnny Mathis reached number 23 on Billboard{{'}}s Easy Listening chart and "bubbled under" the Billboard Hot 100 chart to number 111 in 1968.
*Jamie Redfern peaked at number 9 on the Go-Set Australian charts in 1973.
